title: This commencement season, let's debate A Portrait of a Graduate
author: Mike Petrilli
summary: Mike Petrilli's commencement-season roundup frames the 'Portrait of a Graduate' movement as a site of contested values in K-12 education. The piece features competing takes from practitioners and researchers: Dan Buck and Chad Gestson offer visions for what high school graduates should know and be able to do; Nat Malkus and Marc Porter Magee provide a sobering look at Education Scorecard results; Andy Smarick and Greg Ashman discuss AI in the classroom. The central question -- what is a 'portrait of a graduate' for? -- surfaces tensions between competency-based, holistic, and academic-knowledge-centered visions of secondary education. The AI discussion threads through: whether to teach students to work with AI tools or develop capacities AI cannot replicate is now a live curricular question. Petrilli frames the stakes personally: his own son is graduating high school during the writing of this piece.
points: * The 'Portrait of a Graduate' movement defines student success holistically -- skills, dispositions, citizenship -- rather than through seat time and credit accumulation alone. * Competing visions surface different philosophical commitments: some portraits emphasize knowledge and academic preparation; others foreground social-emotional competencies and civic engagement. * The AI discussion is central: whether to teach students to work with AI tools or develop capacities AI cannot replicate is now a live curricular question. * Education Scorecard data provides a sobering backdrop: academic outcomes remain uneven and improvement is slow despite varied reform efforts. * The roundup format surfaces genuine disagreement among thoughtful practitioners, which is more valuable than consensus-building exercises.
quotes: It's commencement season, including for my firstborn son, who graduates high school in less than two weeks.
So it's a good time to check in on the "portrait of a graduate" movement.

If that term is unfamiliar to you, CASEL defines it as: A holistic look at the skills and competencies students need to master to thrive in work, postsecondary educational opportunities, community, and their personal lives.

Here's how Education Week's Libby Stanford put it a few years ago: Rather than deciding that a student is a successful graduate based on the amount of time they've spent in the classroom, the portrait presents a more well-rounded view of what success looks like.

She also offered some examples: In Kentucky, a successful student is an engaged citizen, critical thinker, effective communicator, empowered learner, creative contributor, and productive collaborator, according to the state's portrait of a learner.

In South Carolina, successful students should be able to read critically, express ideas, investigate through inquiry, reason quantitatively, use sources, design solutions, learn independently, navigate conflict, lead teams, build networks, sustain wellness, and engage as a citizen, according to the state's portrait of a graduate competencies.

And in New York, the proposed portrait , which the state's Board of Regents will vote on in an upcoming meeting, describes a successful graduate as someone who is a critical thinker, innovative problem solver, literate across content areas, culturally competent, social-emotionally competent, an effective communicator, and a global citizen.
